title: Aptamer-functionalized EGCG nanocarrier for neutrophil-targeted AKBA delivery promotes anxiety-related fracture healing

paragraphs.en: Delayed or non-union bone fracture remains one of the most challenging complications in orthopaedics, and its pathogenesis extends far beyond local tissue damage [[1], [2], [3]]. Epidemiological and clinical evidence consistently indicate that patients with comorbid anxiety or depression exhibit greater bone loss, higher fracture incidence, and protracted healing [[4], [5], [6]]. For these patients, already burdened by psychological distress, impaired fracture repair further increases the risk of permanent disability [[7], [8], [9], [10]], worsens long-term functional outcomes, and escalates healthcare costs—a dual physiological and psychological toll that makes this population a pressing target for clinical intervention [[11], [12], [13], [14], [15], [16], [17], [18]]. Yet the molecular mechanisms by which anxiety modulates fracture healing remain largely undefined, and no targeted therapeutic strategy is currently available.

Fracture healing is initiated by a well-orchestrated inflammatory response. Neutrophils, as the first immune cells to arrive at the injury site and launch the repair program, clear necrotic debris and release inflammatory signals, thereby laying the groundwork for subsequent bone regeneration [[19], [20], [21], [22]]. Their functional orientation largely dictates the ultimate course of repair. Within the functionally heterogeneous neutrophil pool, the TGFβ1+CCR5+ double-positive subset has recently been identified as a critical regulator of bone metabolism. This subset is the primary source of TGFβ1 in the mouse bone marrow and is aberrantly expanded in age-related bone loss, directly driving reductions in bone mass. Targeted ablation of this population effectively reverses bone loss, underscoring its centrality as a pathological hub in skeletal homeostasis [23]. However, whether anxiety—a highly prevalent negative emotional state in clinical practice—delays fracture healing through aberrant expansion of this bone-specific pathogenic neutrophil subset remains entirely unknown.

To address this question, we employed a mouse model of CRS-induced anxiety combined with femoral fracture and confirmed that anxiety markedly expanded the TGFβ1+CCR5+ double-positive neutrophil population in the bone marrow, accompanied by overtly impaired fracture healing. This finding positions the pathogenic subset as a potential bridge linking anxiety to defective bone repair. Mechanistically, CRS drives the accumulation of this subset through activation of the NF-κB-CCR5 signaling axis in neutrophils. We next asked whether pharmacological reduction of this subset could rescue healing, and focused on acetyl-11-keto-β-boswellic acid (AKBA) [[24], [25], [26]]. AKBA is a pentacyclic triterpenoid derived from frankincense resin, possessing anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, neuroprotective, and osteogenic-promoting activities, among which its anti-inflammatory and bone-protective properties are particularly relevant to our core question [[27], [28], [29], [30], [31]]. Mechanistic studies revealed that AKBA targets YAP1 to upregulate ubiquitin-specific peptidase 31 (USP31), which in turn suppresses NF-κB phosphorylation and CCR5 expression, thereby significantly reducing the TGFβ1+CCR5+ neutrophil fraction and restoring the osteogenic differentiation capacity of BMSCs.

However, the poor water solubility, low bioavailability, and lack of tissue selectivity of AKBA severely limit its in vivo efficacy. To overcome these obstacles, we designed a NIMP-R14 aptamer-modified nanocarrier system with an epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG) shell (AKBA@E-N), which enables enhanced neutrophil uptake and microenvironment-responsive release of AKBA. In vivo experiments confirmed that this strategy effectively accelerates fracture healing in anxious mice. These results indicate that targeted elimination of the TGFβ1+CCR5+ pathogenic neutrophil subset represents a viable route to rescue anxiety-associated fracture delay. Collectively, this study elucidates a novel mechanism underlying anxiety-related delayed fracture healing and offers a strategy with promising translational therapeutic potential (Scheme 1).

Seven-week-old specific pathogen-free (SPF) male C57BL/6J mice with matched body weight were used in this study and housed under standard laboratory conditions. A CRS protocol was applied to establish the mouse anxiety model, which is widely used for studying anxiety and depression related psychosomatic disorders. Before modeling, all mice underwent an open-field test to assess spontaneous locomotor activity, and animals with activity levels outside the 95% confidence interval were excluded. The screened mice were randomly assigned to the control and CRS groups. Mice in the control group received routine feeding, while those in the CRS group underwent 4 h of daily restraint at 12:00 for 14 consecutive days. For restraint, mice were placed head-down into 50 mL centrifuge tubes perforated with dozens of 2 mm ventilation holes, and the tubes were fixed horizontally on a flat surface to ensure ventilation and stable restraint. Body weight measurement and behavioral tests were performed on day 14 to verify the successful establishment of the anxiety model.

After the CRS model was successfully constructed, all mice received unilateral femoral fracture surgery. Mice were anesthetized by intraperitoneal injection of 1% sodium pentobarbital. After skin preparation and disinfection of the right hind limb, a longitudinal incision was made at the medial mid-femur, and soft tissues were bluntly dissected to expose the femur. A stable closed transverse fracture was created at the femoral mid-shaft with bone rongeurs while preserving the periosteum, followed by intramedullary fixation using a 0.3–0.5 mm Kirschner wire. The incision was closed layer by layer after confirming adequate alignment of the fracture ends. Postoperatively, mice were housed individually with routine wound care and anti-infective treatment. An X-ray was performed to confirm a clear fracture line, stable internal fixation, and no obvious displacement, indicating successful fracture modeling. Mice were monitored daily for wound healing, food/water intake, limb mobility, and signs of infection. Animals with wound suppuration, severe fracture displacement, or inability to feed were immediately euthanized per predefined humane endpoints.

Mice meeting any of the following criteria were immediately humanely euthanized: (1) body weight loss >20% within 7 days; (2) severe wound infection with tissue necrosis; (3) complete loss of ambulatory function due to fracture malposition; (4) persistent pain unresponsive to analgesic treatment; (5) moribund state with hypothermia, unresponsiveness, or respiratory depression. At the experimental endpoint or when humane endpoints were triggered, mice were first deeply anesthetized with 5% isoflurane inhalation, followed by intraperitoneal injection of an overdose of sodium pentobarbital (150 mg/kg). Death was confirmed by permanent cessation of heartbeat and respiration, and tissue samples were collected immediately thereafter.

Following CRS exposure, peripheral blood specimens were collected on days 0, 7, 14, and 21. Sampling was conducted during the midpoint of the mice's nocturnal inactive phase. Within this time window, basal corticosterone (CORT) and norepinephrine (NE) concentrations remain relatively steady, facilitating sensitive identification of stress-provoked hormonal alterations (n = 6 per group; 0.8 ± 0.1 mL of blood collected per mouse). Fresh whole blood was immediately centrifuged at 3000 g for 10 min under 4 °C to isolate serum for subsequent hormone measurement. Serum adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), corticosterone, epinephrine (EPI), and NE concentrations were quantified via commercially available ELISA kits. Assay kits were obtained from Aifang Biotech (Changsha, China), including CORT (AF2061-A) and NE (AF2533-A). All ELISA procedures were performed in strict accordance with the manufacturer's protocols.

At 21 days after fracture surgery, all mice were euthanized via intraperitoneal injection of 150 mg/kg sodium pentobarbital. The fractured right femur was harvested, stripped of adherent soft tissues, fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 24 h, and stored in phosphate-buffered saline at 4 °C prior to micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) scanning.(1)Micro-CT scanning parameters. Scanning was performed on a desktop micro-CT system with consistent parameter settings across all samples: tube voltage of 80 kV, tube current of 100 μA, isotropic voxel resolution of 10 μm, 0.5 mm aluminum filter for beam hardening reduction, 360° full rotation with a 0.5° rotation step, and 300 ms exposure time per frame.(2)Image reconstruction and calibration. Raw projection data were reconstructed into serial transverse 2D slices using the manufacturer's dedicated reconstruction software, with ring artifact correction and beam hardening correction enabled during reconstruction. A standard hydroxyapatite (HA) phantom with two predefined mineral density gradients was scanned under identical parameters to calibrate grayscale values to absolute bone mineral density (BMD), ensuring quantitative comparability across all samples.(3)Definition of region of interest (ROI) and anatomical boundaries. The ROI for quantitative callus analysis was strictly delineated using consistent anatomical landmarks. First, the midpoint of the fracture gap was identified on consecutive coronal and sagittal reformatted slices as the central anatomical reference. The ROI was then defined as a 3 mm-long cylindrical volume extending 1.5 mm proximally and 1.5 mm distally from the fracture line, which fully encompassed all periosteal and endosteal callus tissue. The intact mature cortical bone at both ends far from the fracture site was deliberately excluded from the ROI to avoid interference from native bone.(4)Thresholding strategy and quantitative analysis. A fixed global thresholding approach was adopted to segment mineralized bone tissue from surrounding soft tissue, marrow space, and non-mineralized callus. Based on HA phantom calibration, the grayscale threshold corresponding to 700 Hounsfield Units (HU) was uniformly applied to all samples for mineralized callus segmentation. All ROI delineation and threshold setting were performed by two independent researchers in a blinded manner to minimize measurement bias.

First, the midpoint of the fracture gap was identified on consecutive coronal and sagittal reformatted slices as the central anatomical reference. The ROI was then defined as a 3 mm-long cylindrical volume extending 1.5 mm proximally and 1.5 mm distally from the fracture line, which fully encompassed all periosteal and endosteal callus tissue. The intact mature cortical bone at both ends far from the fracture site was deliberately excluded from the ROI to avoid interference from native bone.

Thresholding strategy and quantitative analysis. A fixed global thresholding approach was adopted to segment mineralized bone tissue from surrounding soft tissue, marrow space, and non-mineralized callus. Based on HA phantom calibration, the grayscale threshold corresponding to 700 Hounsfield Units (HU) was uniformly applied to all samples for mineralized callus segmentation. All ROI delineation and threshold setting were performed by two independent researchers in a blinded manner to minimize measurement bias.

Three-dimensional reconstruction of the ROI was generated for morphological visualization, and three core parameters were quantified to evaluate fracture healing: (1) bone volume fraction (BV/TV, %), calculated as the ratio of mineralized callus volume to total tissue volume within the ROI; (2) bone mineral density (BMD, g/cm3), calibrated to reflect the mineralization level of newly formed bone. All quantitative data were exported from the built-in analysis module of the micro-CT system.

All behavioral tests were performed on the same cohort of mice after 14 days of CRS exposure and before fracture surgery, following a standardized protocol to minimize cross-paradigm stress carryover effects. Tests were administered in ascending order of stress intensity, with a minimum 24-h rest interval between independent assays. All tests were conducted during the late light phase under consistent illumination (200 lux) and temperature (22 ± 1 °C). The apparatus was thoroughly cleaned with 75% ethanol between animals to eliminate residual olfactory cues, and all behavioral data were quantified by two blinded researchers. The tests were performed in the following order: (1) Open Field Test (OFT) on Day 14, (2) Elevated Plus Maze (EPM) on Day 15, (3) Sucrose Preference Test (SPT) on Days 16–18 (with 48-h habituation and 12-h food deprivation prior to testing), (4) Forced Swimming Test (FST) on Day 19 (with a 15-min pretest on Day 18), and (5) Tail Suspension Test (TST) on Day 20. This sequential order ensures that anxiety-related tests (OFT, EPM) are completed before the more stressful depression-related tests (FST, TST), thereby minimizing carryover stress effects. Using one week as a cycle, OFT was repeated in sequence on days 21 and 28, and all behavioral tests were performed across three cycles.

Elevated Plus Maze (EPM): Anxiety-like behaviors were assessed using an elevated plus maze with 30–35 cm-long arms, 5 cm wide, and 50–60 cm high, under 100–300 lux illumination. Mice were acclimated for 30 min before testing and then placed in the maze center, facing an open arm. Activity was recorded for 5 min, and anxiety levels were quantified as the percentage of time spent and entries in the open arms. The maze was sanitized with 75% ethanol between tests, and all assays were performed during the light phase.

Open Field Test (OFT): Locomotor activity and anxiety were evaluated in a 500 mm × 500 mm × 415 mm enclosed arena, with behavior recorded by an overhead camera. Mice were acclimated for 7 days with daily handling, then transferred to the test room 1 h before experimentation. After placement in the arena center, movement was tracked for 15 min. Total distance traveled, central zone entries, and residence time were analyzed automatically in a double-blinded manner. Abnormally active mice were excluded, and OFT was conducted first.

Forced Swimming Test (FST): Depressive-like behaviors were measured over two days. On day 1, mice swam for 15 min in water (25–30 °C, 10 cm depth) and were dried before being returned to their cages. On day 2, mice were tested for 6 min, and immobility time during the last 4 min was recorded as a marker of depressive behavior. Tests were performed at fixed times in the same season to control for environmental variables.

Tail Suspension Test (TST): Mice were acclimated for 30 min, then suspended 50 cm above the floor by adhesive tape 1 cm from the tail tip. Behavior was recorded for 6 min under dim light, and immobility time in the last 4 min was quantified to indicate depressive-like behaviors. Assays were performed at a fixed circadian time to avoid timing bias.

Sucrose Preference Test (SPT): Individually housed mice were acclimated to 1% sucrose solution and distilled water for 48 h, with bottle positions swapped every 12 h. After 12 h of food deprivation, liquid consumption was measured at 0, 12, 24, and 36 h. The sucrose preference coefficient was calculated as (sucrose intake/total fluid intake) × 100%, with lower values indicating anhedonia.

Neutrophils were isolated from mouse bone marrow using a commercial mouse bone marrow neutrophil isolation kit (Haoyang Bio). All procedures were performed in a sterile environment at 18–22 °C and completed within 2 h after sample collection. Following euthanasia, mouse femurs or tibias were dissected, and both ends of the bones were transected. Bone marrow was flushed from the medullary cavity using homogenate washing buffer to obtain a cell suspension. The suspension was filtered through a 70 μm cell strainer and centrifuged at 450×g for 10 min. The resulting cell pellet was resuspended in red blood cell lysis buffer to a final concentration of 2×108–1×109 cells/mL. The 80% isolation solution was prepared by mixing Isolation Solution 1 and tissue sample dilution buffer at a ratio of 4:1. According to the sample volume (0.5–3.0 mL), Isolation Solution 1 and the prepared 80% isolation solution were sequentially added into sterile centrifuge tubes to form a density gradient. The cell suspension was slowly overlaid onto the gradient surface, then centrifuged at 450–600×g for 30 min. The third milky-white, ring-shaped neutrophil layer was carefully aspirated. The harvested neutrophils were washed with 5–10 mL of washing buffer and subjected to two sequential centrifugation cycles (400×g for 10 min, then 250×g for 10 min). Finally, the cells were resuspended in 0.5 mL of washing buffer or the desired experimental solution.

TGFβ1+CCR5+ double-positive neutrophils were isolated from mouse bone marrow by a two-step MACS procedure following a previously established protocol [23]. Briefly, bone marrow cells were sequentially incubated with biotinylated anti-CCR5 and anti-TGFβ1 antibodies (BioLegend), followed by anti-biotin microbeads (Miltenyi Biotec) and positive selection using LS columns (Miltenyi Biotec). All procedures were performed at 4 °C to preserve cell viability.

An in vitro co-culture system of primary neutrophils and BMSCs were established using Transwell chambers. Primary neutrophils were seeded in the upper chamber, and BMSCs were cultured in the lower chamber. Before co-culture, BMSCs were plated at a density of 5 × 104 cells per well and cultured in complete medium until adherence and confluence. Primary mouse neutrophils were isolated by MACS, and the cell concentration was adjusted immediately after sorting for seeding into the upper Transwell chambers. The chambers were then transferred to the culture plates pre-seeded with BMSCs, and an equal volume of medium was added to maintain consistent liquid levels, initiating co-culture. Given that primary mouse neutrophils lack proliferative capacity in vitro and undergo rapid apoptosis within 24 h, the total co-culture duration was strictly controlled at 21.5 h. To ensure experimental stability, primary neutrophils were freshly isolated daily, and those in the upper Transwell chambers were promptly replaced after MACS to avoid interference from cell apoptosis.

Purified primary neutrophils obtained by magnetic-activated cell sorting were collected in EP tubes and fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde at room temperature for 15 min. After washing, cells were permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100 at room temperature and then blocked in PBS containing 5% bovine serum albumin (BSA) for 1 h to prevent non-specific binding. Cells were incubated with diluted rabbit anti-mouse CCR5 primary antibody (Servicebio, GB11504-100, 1:200 in PBS containing 1% BSA) at 4 °C overnight. The next day, a fluorescently labeled secondary antibody (Cy3-labeled goat anti-rabbit IgG, 1:200) was added and incubated for 50 min at room temperature in the dark. After three washes with PBS for 5 min each, rabbit anti-mouse TGFβ1 primary antibody (Proteintech, Cat No. 81746-2-RR, 1:150) was labeled with FITC using the FITC labeling kit (Proteintech, Cat No.: KFA501) and then incubated with cells for 50 min. Subsequently, cells were stained with DAPI staining solution for 15 min at room temperature in the dark to label nuclei. An anti-fade mounting medium was added, and 10 μL of the cell suspension was placed on a glass slide and covered with a coverslip. Images were captured with a laser-scanning confocal microscope using a 100× oil-immersion objective, with excitation wavelengths of 488 nm (FITC), 555 nm (Cy3), and 405 nm (DAPI). Z-stack scanning was performed to confirm fluorescence localization. The co-expression of TGFβ1 and CCR5 was analyzed using merged images, and the proportion of double-positive cells was quantified in ImageJ. All procedures were performed in the dark. A negative control without primary antibody was set to exclude non-specific fluorescence interference.

Five distinct sample types were prepared for qRT-PCR quantification: MACS-sorted bone marrow neutrophils, in vitro-cultured BMSCs, in vivo fracture callus tissues, Hoxb8 cells, and HL-60 cells with specific sampling sites and isolation procedures described separately below.(1)MACS-sorted TGFβ1+CCR5+ neutrophils (for detection of Usp31, Ccr5, Tgfβ1 and inflammatory axis genes). After euthanasia of mice, bilateral femurs and tibiae were sterilely dissected as the exact sampling sites of bone marrow. Both bone epiphyseal ends were cut off, and bone marrow was flushed out with pre-cooled PBS to prepare a single-cell suspension. TGFβ1+CCR5+ double-positive neutrophils were purified via two-step MACS separation as described in Section 4. Purified cell pellets were collected by centrifugation and immediately lysed with TRIzol reagent for total RNA extraction. Only cell populations with sorting purity ≥78% were subjected to subsequent transcriptional detection.(2)In vitro co-cultured BMSCs (for detection of osteogenic markers Runx2, Col1a1, Bglap). BMSCs grown on the lower chamber of Transwell co-culture systems were used without in vivo tissue sampling. Culture medium was discarded, and adherent BMSCs were washed three times with pre-cooled PBS, scraped off, and lysed with TRIzol to isolate cellular RNA.(3)Fracture callus tissues from in vivo mouse models (for in vivo osteogenic gene quantification). The sampling site was limited to newly formed callus tissue within 1 mm above and below the femoral fracture line, with mature cortical bone at both fracture ends completely excluded. Fresh callus was dissected under a stereomicroscope immediately after animal sacrifice, snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen, and ground into powder prior to TRIzol-mediated total RNA extraction.(4)Hoxb8 cells. After washing with PBS, it was used for subsequent operations.(5)HL-60 cells. After washing with PBS, it was used for subsequent operations.

After RNA extraction, the purity and integrity of total RNA were verified by Nanodrop spectrophotometry (A260/A280 = 1.8–2.1) and agarose gel electrophoresis to exclude RNA degradation. Qualified RNA samples were reverse-transcribed into complementary DNA (cDNA) using an Invitrogen reverse transcription kit following manufacturer's instructions. Quantitative real-time PCR was performed on a Vazymebiotech qPCR instrument with gene-specific primers listed in the table, and β-actin was set as the housekeeping reference gene for all five sample categories. Each biological sample was arranged with 3 technical replicates, and all experiments were independently repeated for 3 biological batches.
